doc.title: Cedar Walton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Politics and social content in his music
summary: Asked about Abbey and Max's protest sensibility, Walton says his instrumental music is more like science and not programmatic, except The Maestro, a story about Ellington.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: How did that sensibility work itself into your music, if it has?

Oh, I uh, don't have a good answer for that because uh, what I do musically I uh, I can't uh, uh, incorporate anything socially uh, really that I can tell you. Uh, I'd have to think about that. I, I can't just, I don't have uh, uh, uh, uh, a real, uh, motivation to, to do that in the first place. I mean, to, you know, and it's a great question, mind you, and I think there's a lot of answers from a lot of composers. But I, uh, I don't, I think uh, instrumentally, it's, it's uh, it's uh, more like a science as compared to a movement to me. Freedom Now Suite, I think, had uh, uh, all kinda vocals in it, uh, you know, expressing uh, this uh, period in American history. But uh, my music is instrumental, it's not uh … except …

No, with the exception of The Maestro, and it's about Duke Ellington. It's not uh, social, socially significant, I don't think, you know, except a story about one man and his uh, contribution to, to, to music history.
